What Is a Computer-Use Agent?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 26 September 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

A computer-use agent is an AI agent that operates software the way a person does: it looks at screenshots and decides where to click, what to type and when to scroll. It can work in applications that have no API or connector. It is also slower, less reliable and more exposed to manipulation than an agent working through APIs. Providers advise running it on an isolated machine with minimal access, and asking a person to confirm anything with real-world consequences.

What a computer-use agent means

Most agents act through function calls: structured requests to an API, a database or an MCP server. A computer-use agent acts through the screen. Microsoft's documentation describes the loop in three stages. Perception captures a screenshot. Reasoning judges the current state against the goal. Action clicks, types or scrolls. The loop repeats until the task is done or needs a person.

Anthropic's documentation is explicit that the model never touches the machine. The application receives the model's requests, translates them into actions in its own computing environment, captures screenshots and returns them. The available actions include taking a screenshot, zooming, clicking, dragging, scrolling, typing and pressing keys.

API-based agentComputer-use agentRPA robot
How it actsStructured calls to APIs and toolsClicks and keystrokes chosen from screenshotsScripted clicks and keystrokes
Needs an APIYesNoNo
When a screen changesNot affectedOften copes, by reading the new screenUsually breaks
SpeedFastSlowFast
PredictabilityHighLow to mediumHigh

Why it matters for a commercial team

The appeal is reach. Many commercial teams still depend on systems with no usable API, such as a partner portal or an old quoting tool. Microsoft describes computer use as "especially useful in scenarios where APIs aren't available". Unlike robotic process automation, it can cope with a button that has moved.

The evidence on reliability is sobering. OSWorld tested agents on 369 tasks in real operating systems and applications. At publication in April 2024, humans completed 72.36% and the best model 12.24%. Most failures came from locating elements on screen and from operational knowledge. OpenAI's Computer-Using Agent, announced in January 2025, reached 38.1% on OSWorld and 58.1% on the browser benchmark WebArena, against human scores of 72.4% and 78.2%. Scores have risen since, but public benchmarks rarely match a firm's own screens.

Providers' own limitations lists agree. Anthropic warns that the model "might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates", that reliability may be lower in niche applications, and that it may be too slow compared with a person. Microsoft notes its tool can struggle with dropdowns, date pickers and custom widgets, and "might repeat actions or get stuck". In OpenAI's own examples, one text-editing task succeeded 4 times in 10.

It is also costly in tokens. Anthropic's pricing page, accessed 16 November 2026, lists about 4,520 tokens of overhead for its computer-use toolset definition, before any screenshots are added.

Security is the larger issue. A computer-use agent reads everything on screen, including text placed there by others. Anthropic's documentation states that instructions on webpages or in images "might override your instructions". It now scans screenshots with classifiers for prompt injection, but says its other precautions remain important. Microsoft warns that pauses for clarification "might not trigger in every situation where a person would want a pause", and that they should not be relied on as a fail-safe.

This is why lowob places computer use low on the autonomy dial. Reading a portal and drafting what it found is level 0 or 1. Submitting an order, a form or a message has consequences, so it sits at level 2 at most, with a named person approving each one. OpenAI's agent asked for confirmation before submitting orders or sending email and declined banking transactions. Anthropic advises confirmation before financial transactions or agreeing to terms of service.

How to pilot one safely

ControlWhat it means in practice
Isolated machineA dedicated virtual machine or container, never a person's own laptop
Least-privilege accountIts own login, read-only where possible; see agent identity
No credentials in reachAnthropic advises against giving the model login details
Domain allowlistOnly the sites the task needs
Approval before submitA person confirms every form, order or message at an approval gate
Logs and screenshots keptEvery action reviewable after the run
API firstIf an API or connector exists, use it instead

Start with a read-only task, such as collecting order status from a partner portal into a draft summary.

lowob takeaways

  • It works through the screen. Screenshots in, clicks and keystrokes out.
  • Reach comes at a price. Slower and less reliable than API-based agents.
  • The screen can carry instructions. Treat on-screen content as untrusted.
  • Isolate it and gate its actions. A separate machine, minimal access and a person approving every submission.

Common questions

What is the difference between a computer-use agent and RPA?

RPA follows a recorded script and breaks when a screen changes. A computer-use agent decides each step from a screenshot, so it adapts to changes but is slower and less predictable.

How accurate are computer-use agents?

Below human level on public benchmarks. OSWorld's original paper reported 12.24% for the best model against over 72% for humans, and OpenAI reported 38.1% for its agent in January 2025. Test on your own tasks.

Is it safe to let an AI agent use my computer?

Not directly. Providers advise a dedicated virtual machine with minimal privileges, no stored credentials, a domain allowlist and human confirmation for consequential actions.

When should I use computer use instead of an API?

Only when no API or connector exists and the task cannot wait for one. Where an API exists, it is faster, uses fewer tokens and is easier to control.
